opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the funny thing about distillation is that everyone thinks of it as this old, solved idea. Hinton's paper came out in 2015, you train a small student to match the soft labels of a big teacher, and that's it. But when you look at how people were actually building models, especially in the last couple of years, distillation was quietly doing a huge amount of the heavy lifting. Smaller models like Gemma or the Flash-style models get a lot of their quality from learning off a stronger teacher, and the community at large was doing it too, just fine-tuning on outputs generated by GPT-4 or other frontier models. That's distillation, even if people didn't always call it that.

So part of the motivation was simply that there was a gap between how important the technique had become in practice and how well people understood it. A lot of folks were doing the most naive version: sample a bunch of outputs from the teacher, do supervised fine-tuning on them, done. And that works okay, but it has real problems. The biggest one is the train-test mismatch. During training the student only ever sees sequences the teacher generated, but at inference time it has to condition on its own generations, which can drift into places the teacher never went. Small errors compound, and the student doesn't know how to recover.

That was a big part of what we'd been working on, things like on-policy distillation, where you let the student generate and then have the teacher give feedback on the student's own samples, token by token. It's conceptually close to imitation learning ideas like DAgger, and it ties distillation much more closely to RL. Once you see it that way, you realize there's a whole design space: which divergence you minimize, forward KL versus reverse KL, whether data is on-policy or off-policy, how you mix in rewards. Those choices actually matter a lot for the final model.

So the tutorial felt worthwhile because, one, it's a technique almost every lab depends on; two, the standard recipe leaves a lot on the table; and three, there's a really nice unifying story connecting distillation, imitation learning, and RL that I don't think was widely appreciated. If you're trying to get the best small model you possibly can, which is what most people deploying things actually care about, understanding distillation properly is one of the highest-leverage things you can do.

r001.rationale: The response moves from the original soft-label teacher–student recipe to LLM distillation, but never identifies the earlier focus as classifier distillation.

r002.rationale: It describes on-policy distillation as closely related to imitation learning such as DAgger and connected to RL, showing inspiration from approaches beyond conventional distillation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started from a feeling that distillation had become one of those techniques everyone uses and almost nobody thinks about anymore. It's twenty-plus years old if you go back to model compression, ten years old if you count from the Hinton paper, and it's quietly sitting inside basically every production model today. Gemini Flash, the small Llama models, the reasoning models people are running locally. All of them are distilled from something bigger. But if you ask people how it works, you get the textbook answer: train the student on the teacher's soft labels, done.

And that answer is just wrong for language models, or at least badly incomplete. The thing that actually got me interested was noticing that the way practitioners do distillation and the way the textbook describes it had drifted apart. In practice, most people are doing sequence-level distillation. You sample outputs from the teacher and fine-tune the student on them. That's supervised fine-tuning on synthetic data. Nobody calls it distillation, but that's what it is. And then there's the token-level version with logits, which is what people think of as "real" distillation, and the two have very different properties, very different failure modes, and almost no one had laid out when you'd want one versus the other.

The other motivation was that my own work on on-policy distillation had convinced me that the data distribution matters more than the loss function. If the student only ever sees teacher-generated sequences, it never learns to recover from its own mistakes. It makes one error early in a generation and it's in territory the teacher never showed it. Once you frame it that way, distillation starts looking much more like reinforcement learning than like supervised learning, and that connection reframes a lot of things. The teacher becomes a dense reward signal rather than a label source.

So the tutorial was partly me trying to organize my own understanding, and partly a bet that this would get a lot more important rather than less. Inference costs are the thing that actually constrains deployment now. The big frontier models are increasingly a means to an end, and the end is a cheaper model that behaves like them. If that's where the field is going, then the question of how you transfer capability from a large model to a small one deserves to be treated as a first-class research problem, not a post-processing step. That seemed worth an afternoon of everyone's time.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts textbook soft-label distillation with language-model practice, but does not identify a shift from classifier-focused distillation to LLM distillation as the reason to revisit the topic.

r002.rationale: It describes on-policy distillation as resembling reinforcement learning, with the teacher serving as a dense reward signal rather than a label source—an approach distinct from conventional distillation.

astra-6.text:
I think distillation is one of those ideas that’s been around long enough that people assume it’s a solved problem. You have a big teacher, you train a smaller student to imitate it, and that’s the story. But with language models, there are some important choices hidden in that description. What data does the student learn from? Is it learning on outputs generated by the teacher, or on outputs it would actually produce itself?

That distinction matters because the student makes different mistakes than the teacher. If it only sees the teacher’s trajectories during training, it may never learn how to handle the situations it encounters at inference time. So I thought it was worth revisiting distillation as a learning problem, rather than just a compression technique, and building intuition for when the different approaches should work.

r001.rationale: The response says language models introduce important distillation choices, but does not identify a shift from classifier-focused distillation to LLM distillation.

r002.rationale: The response discusses teacher-generated versus student-generated training data, but does not say recent distillation methods draw inspiration from approaches unlike conventional distillation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think distillation is one of those ideas that’s simple to describe, but has a lot more depth than people initially appreciate. You have a teacher model, and you use its outputs to train a student. But what should the teacher generate? Which examples should you train on? And what happens when the student starts making mistakes that the teacher wouldn’t make?

So the motivation for revisiting it was to unpack those choices. Especially with language models, distillation is more than just compressing a large model into a smaller one. It’s a way of transferring capabilities, and the details of that transfer can really matter.

r001.rationale: The response says distillation has particular relevance for language models, but it does not identify a shift from classifier-focused distillation to LLM distillation.

r002.rationale: It discusses choices in teacher outputs, training examples, and student errors, but does not say recent methods draw on approaches unlike conventional distillation.
